title: Day 0 - Primer
headline: CODEBREAKER'S PRIMER
subheadline: Training cipher for new agents. Work the five tells in order: single-letter words, frequent letters, short words, apostrophes, then double letters. Tap a glyph and type — every copy of that glyph fills at once. For your first exercise, decode this standard training phrase designed to test your eye for common grammar patterns and identical consecutive characters.
originalText: I CAN'T SEE THE WORD THE AND LOOK AT A DOUBLE LETTER TOO.

hints.clue: A drill that names the tells it wants you to hunt.

title: Day 1 - Easy
headline: TRAGEDY AT THE VANCE ESTATE
subheadline: High society was rocked last night when Archibald Vance, the renowned railroad and shipping tycoon, was discovered deceased in his locked study during his annual gala. Thorne noted the absence of a weapon, yet a distinct, unnatural scent lingered in the stale air. A single crystal coupe glass sat perfectly centered on the mahogany desk, and a crumpled draft of a telegraph was recovered from Vance's tuxedo pocket. The medical examiner is baffled, but my gut says murder. What did the tycoon ingest, and what was he trying to send before his heart stopped? A closer look at the crystal coupe suggests the deadly concoction wasn't poured from the main bar, but slipped into a celebratory toast.
originalText: THE FATAL DOSE WAS IN THE CHAMPAGNE.

hints.clue: The coupe on the desk held more than bubbles.

title: Day 1 - Hard
headline: THE TUXEDO TELEGRAPH
subheadline: NIGHT EXTRA — The paper found in Vance's pocket was recovered from the wire room after deadline. It proves the old man wasn't just sipping drinks—he was going to war. The late-city transmission is still in cipher. The decoded wire reveals Archibald's final, desperate promise to tear down his own empire by shining a light on his partners' sins.
originalText: HE THREATENED TO EXPOSE US ALL.

hints.clue: The tuxedo paper was a warning, not a toast.

title: Day 2 - Easy
headline: THE WIDOW'S LAMENT
subheadline: I interviewed Beatrice Vance this morning. The grieving widow was dressed in immaculate black silk, her eyes dry and her demeanor as cold as ice. She claims she was dancing with her husband's business partner at the exact time of the murder. But the upstairs maid confided in me that Beatrice and Archibald had a vicious, hushed argument just hours before the guests arrived. I found a charred scrap of heavy parchment near the fireplace in Beatrice's boudoir. It seems the flames didn't quite finish their job hiding her secrets. The heavy, watermarked paper bears the distinct seal of a law office. Archibald left a copy of the revocation on the study desk where she would snoop during the gala. She thought she was being clever, stealing it and feeding it to the grate before the lawyer ever read a will. She was destroying Archibald's revocation of the 1923 corporate handover. She thought burning it would keep the shipping fleet in the Syndicate's hands forever, entirely unaware that the old man had already set a deeper, deadlier trap, and that the scrap would point her—and me—at the wall.
originalText: HE CHANGED THE WILL BEFORE THE GALA.

hints.clue: The grate did not finish a lawyer's page.

title: Day 2 - Hard
headline: THE SCORCHED FRAME
subheadline: LATE CITY FINAL — Following the burned fragment's lead, detectives forced the library at dusk. The scrap points at a painted hull on the wall because he aimed it there. She thought she was covering her tracks. He left her a breadcrumb. Whatever sits behind it is not a love nest. It is the paper trail of the fleet and patents she thought the burned revocation had already locked in for the Syndicate.
originalText: A COMPARTMENT BEHIND THE RED SAILBOAT.

hints.clue: The scrap on the hearth pointed at a painted hull.

title: Day 3 - Easy
headline: A MISSING HEIR
subheadline: Whispers echo through the hallowed halls of the Vance estate today following the reading of the late millionaire’s will. The lawyer revealed a shocking twist regarding the bulk of the massive fortune. The room erupted into chaos, and Arthur Sterling abruptly left the premises looking as pale as a man who had just seen a ghost. Our sources indicate a frantic search is underway. The police intercepted an unsigned postcard today, bearing a typed address to Sterling's office and a block of garbled text. It seems to be a desperate update sent to Sterling’s office from a shadow on the payroll. Rumors have long circulated about a young female ward hidden away from the public eye, and this garbled text provides a glimmer of hope that there is still life left in the heiress's lungs.
originalText: THE GIRL IS STILL BREATHING.

hints.clue: The unsigned card was not an obituary.

title: Day 3 - Hard
headline: THE ALBANY STUB
subheadline: NIGHT EXTRA — The sun has set on the will reading. Sterling is not answering his door, but a night clerk at Grand Central sold the precinct a piece of paper recovered after the last train rolled out. This late dispatch is still in cipher. The scrap appears to be a transit receipt, confirming someone was quietly shipped north on a clandestine rail line.
originalText: BOUGHT HER A ONE WAY TICKET UPSTATE.

hints.clue: A night clerk sold a stub that ran north.

title: Day 4 - Easy
headline: SHADOWS IN THE OFFICE
subheadline: A midnight call roused me from what little slumber I had managed since the gala. A crew in Sterling’s pay broke into the Vance & Sterling Shipping Co. downtown. Curiously, they weren't after cash—the company safe was untouched. Instead, specific filing cabinets were stripped to the wood. Whatever Sterling is hiding, it involves the ghosts of the past. On the floor beneath the shattered window, I found a train ticket stub to Albany with a hastily scrawled coded message on the back—a directive from the men who scrubbed the files. The missing folders specifically held the company's maritime shipping manifests dating back exactly three years.
originalText: HIDING THE NINETEEN TWENTY THREE VOYAGES.

hints.clue: They left the safe and emptied the three-year cabinets.

title: Day 4 - Hard
headline: THE EMPTIED CABINETS
subheadline: LATE CITY FINAL — Harbor watchmen swear The Midnight Runner takes on unmarked crates after the lights go out. A second cipher from the emptied logs has not been typeset. The cipher hints that the so-called textile shipments from Havana were actually a clever front for highly profitable, sloshy contraband.
originalText: THE CUBAN SILK IS LIQUID GOLD.

hints.clue: Those Havana crates were never cut for a dressmaker.

title: Day 5 - Easy
headline: AN INTERCEPTED WIRE
subheadline: A stroke of luck. Our boys down at the telegraph office intercepted a message sent by Arthur Sterling to a mysterious "Mr. Black" at a private club in Albany. Sterling has been sweating bullets since the will reading, pacing his study until all hours. Beatrice Vance has also been seen entering Sterling’s estate through the servant's entrance. The telegraph operator managed to copy down two segments of the transmission before the line was suspiciously cut. In the first segment, Beatrice drops the grieving widow act and issues a hostile, frantic demand to Sterling. We must decode the rest immediately to intercept the courier. The fragment catches the widow demanding her cut of the illicit profits be delivered immediately to a high-end Manhattan hotel.
originalText: SEND MY HALF TO THE PLAZA.

hints.clue: The widow dropped the veil and named a hotel desk.

title: Day 5 - Hard
headline: THE DEAD WIRE
subheadline: NIGHT EXTRA — The line went dead at 11:47 p.m. Blackwood knew his captive was already gone, but he played his hand cold, squeezing Sterling for one last payout before the house of cards collapsed.
originalText: PAY THE CLINIC OR SHE WALKS.

hints.clue: The dead wire was a ransom, not a condolence.

title: Day 6 - Easy
headline: THE DOCTOR'S SECRET
subheadline:
(Journal Entry - Detective Elias Thorne, Sept 9, 1926)
Three days on nothing but black coffee, Lucky Strikes, and a sleeping car to Albany. Four hours north. Too far for a gala toast. I stumbled off the platform in a rumpled suit, eyes bloodshot, following the ticket stub trail to the Blackwood Sanatorium. The head physician, Dr. Aris Blackwood, was remarkably uncooperative, insisting patient records were confidential and that Clara was resting securely in the west wing. I clocked him as a sleazy upstate jailer on Sterling's payroll, not a man who could have been in that locked study. The murder is a Manhattan job. This is just where they stashed the girl. His desk was littered with Beatrice’s perfumed letters. However, a sympathetic nurse slipped me a folded napkin as I left the grounds. It seems Dr. Blackwood is lying through his teeth to keep his monthly payments from Vance & Sterling Shipping Co. rolling in. The nurse’s frantic note contained a coded message detailing a sudden, massive problem at the facility. Using a colorful barnyard metaphor, the nurse's hastily scribbled code warns that the doctor's prized captive managed to slip away before the weekend was out.
originalText: THE BIRD FLEW THE COOP ON SUNDAY.

hints.clue: The nurse's napkin used a barnyard word for an empty ward.

title: Day 6 - Hard
headline: THE HOTEL NAPKIN
subheadline: LATE CITY FINAL — After dark, the sympathetic nurse slipped a second item under Detective Thorne’s hotel door: a torn, encoded page from the doctor’s personal ledger. The accounting lines expose a steady supply of heavy narcotics, authorized straight from the top to keep their captive docile. An extortion pipeline. Not a murder kit. Thorne files it under Albany and goes back to hunting Manhattan.
originalText: HEAVY DOSES OF MORPHINE ORDERED BY STERLING.

hints.clue: The hotel ledger was a pharmacy bill, not a murder kit.

title: Day 7 - Easy
headline: THE MIDNIGHT RUNNER
subheadline:
(Newspaper Clipping - The Waterfront Whisperer, Sept 10, 1926)
A suspicious vessel, The Midnight Runner, was raided by the Coast Guard late last night after attempting to slip past the federal blockade at Rum Row. Registered to Vance & Sterling Shipping Co., the cargo manifest claimed it was transporting textiles from Cuba. However, underneath the crates of silk, Volstead Act enforcers uncovered illicit cargo that had nothing to do with textiles. Witnesses say Detective Elias Thorne, still in yesterday’s rumpled suit and looking as though he had not slept since Albany, was already on the pier when the boarding party went over the rail. Dockhands swore they rarely saw Archibald down at the piers. There was a shadow broker calling the shots after sundown, a man who treated the fleet like his own personal toy. Was Archibald murdered to protect a million-dollar bootlegging empire from its rightful owner? A cryptic ledger was found in the captain’s quarters, containing an encoded entry that finally puts a name to the boss. The decoded text strips away the shadows, explicitly naming the surviving partner who now commands the entire smuggling fleet.
originalText: ARTHUR GIVES THE ORDERS NOW.

hints.clue: The captain's book names which partner runs the dark fleet.

title: Day 7 - Hard
headline: THE CAPTAIN'S LEDGER
subheadline: NIGHT EXTRA — Coast Guard papers seized from The Midnight Runner include a second ledger page the morning edition did not print, revealing exactly what triggered the tycoon's murder. The extra page is not a discovery so much as a fuse: the old man's own hand, left where federal men would have to find it, timed to burn the partners who thought he was still in the dark.
originalText: THE OLD MAN PLANTED THE BOOTLEGGING LEDGER AS A TRAP.

hints.clue: The extra page was bait the federal men were meant to find.

title: Day 8 - Easy
headline: THE BUTLER'S CONFESSION
subheadline:
(Police Interrogation Transcript - Sept 11, 1926)
I brought Reginald, the Vance family butler, in for questioning today. He has served the family for twenty years but looked as though he had aged a decade overnight. He finally broke under pressure, admitting he used his master key on the locked study minutes before Archibald Vance was found dead. As the oak door swung in, he caught a scent that was wildly out of place in a tycoon's cigar-smoke-filled sanctuary. When asked who rushed past him in the hall, Reginald clammed up, terrified for his life. A search of his quarters turned up a matchbook from a notorious downtown speakeasy, The Blind Tiger, with two messages scrawled inside. The first hasty scrawl on the matchbook cover reveals the shocking gender of the mysterious figure fleeing the scene of the crime.
originalText: A WOMAN IN THE LOCKED STUDY.

hints.clue: The matchbook scrawl names a gender, not a face.

title: Day 8 - Hard
headline: THE SECOND CONFESSION
subheadline: LATE CITY FINAL — Under lamplight at headquarters the butler recanted part of his story and whispered a longer cipher. He took a wad of cash and would not say whose hand passed it. What he would admit is the lock. Same bolt works both sides: thumb-turn at the desk, master key in the hall. The old man had already thrown it. Reginald drew it back, let them in, threw it shut behind them, then opened it again once the glass had done its work and locked the corpse in for morning. I booked him for the night. By dawn Chief O'Malley will be circling the cage with a story about insufficient evidence. Sterling's badge is already in this building.
originalText: SOMEONE LOCKED THE DEADBOLT FROM THE HALLWAY.

hints.clue: His second story is about which side of the oak threw the bolt.

title: Day 9 - Easy
headline: SECRETS IN THE SAFE
subheadline:
(Journal Entry - Detective Elias Thorne, Sept 12, 1926)
Using the lead decoded from the charred scrap, I located the hidden wall safe behind the library canvas. The first thing that hit the light was not a will. Archibald had pinned a city birth certificate to the inner door with a steel tack and a note in his own hand, placed so any cop who cracked the vault would read it before the ledgers. Beatrice was hunting the company books. He left her a child she had buried. I summoned her to the library and laid it on the mahogany desk. She went white as a sheet. What he locked away wasn't just corporate corruption—it was the lie at the center of his family, aimed to wreck her before the money ever changed hands. The decades-old city record strips away the family's pristine image, exposing a scandalous, hidden truth about the missing heiress's real maternity.
originalText: THE WIDOW IS HER TRUE BIOLOGICAL MOTHER.

hints.clue: Pinned to the vault: a city record that rewrites the family tree.

title: Day 9 - Hard
headline: THE MIDNIGHT INVENTORY
subheadline: NIGHT EXTRA — A midnight inventory of the wall safe produced a second encoded letter in Clara’s hand. The morning paper held this dispatch back. The page still smells of lavender and rage. Memory is coming back in bursts, and she is not writing like a lawyer. She is writing like a daughter who just learned the name of the woman who left her in a ward.
originalText: CLARA VOWED TO EXPOSE HER OWN MOTHER.

hints.clue: The lavender page is a daughter's rage, not a lawyer's brief.

title: Day 10 - Easy
headline: A VOICE FROM THE SHADOWS
subheadline:
(Intercepted Letter - Sept 13, 1926)
A letter arrived at the precinct today, addressed directly to me. It smelled faintly of lavender and damp earth. The handwriting was elegant but frantic. It was from Clara Vance. She reveals she is hiding in plain sight in the city, terrified for her life. She claims her father’s death was just the beginning, and that The Blind Tiger is the center of the conspiracy. She had slipped into a priest-hole behind the bookshelves; the old man never knew she was in the wall. The angle was cruel: she could see only hands, hear a deep voice, and observe one highly distinctive accessory resting against the oak floorboards. The sanatorium narcotics have left her memory in fragments. The man’s face is a blur. She enclosed two ciphers, promising they hold the key to the killer's identity. Across the bottom she scrawled a desperate directive: track down the object mentioned in the code. The cipher explicitly describes this crucial floorboard accessory, pointing squarely to a suspect who requires ornate, metallic assistance to walk. I am hunting a New York phantom. A mobster with a cane. Not the Albany physician I left behind a four-hour train.
originalText: THE KILLER LEANS ON CARVED SILVER.

hints.clue: From the wall she saw an accessory on the oak, not a face.

title: Day 10 - Hard
headline: THE SECOND LETTER
subheadline: LATE CITY FINAL — A second letter arrived after dusk. Clara still cannot name the man with the deep voice. This night extra is the rest of her hand. From the priest-hole she heard the talk first, then the sip: a deep voice, a medicinal smell, a limp on oak. A shadow. Not a face. The old man did not have time to argue after the glass. Thorne hunted Manhattan, not a physician's desk in Albany.
originalText: A DEEP VOICE COAXED THE VICTIM TO DRINK.

hints.clue: She heard the toast before she ever saw the glass.

title: Day 11 - Easy
headline: INTO THE TIGER'S DEN
subheadline:
(Journal Entry - Detective Elias Thorne, Sept 14, 1926)
Following the matchbook clue, I traded my detective's coat for a cheap suit and slinked into The Blind Tiger. The speakeasy was thick with cigar smoke, bathtub gin, and the frantic rhythm of a ragtime band. Through the haze, I spotted Arthur Sterling tucked away in a velvet VIP booth, sweating profusely while whispering with some unfamiliar men who didn't look like shipping magnates. The bartender was acting as their go-between, passing folded notes under cocktail napkins. I swiped one of those napkins during a scuffle. The criminal underground is embedded in Vance's empire, and this cipher details exactly what Sterling is shopping for. The hurried handwriting confirms Sterling isn't just securing his shipping routes—he's actively purchasing brutal, hired thuggery from a notorious local gang.
originalText: BUYING MUSCLE FROM THE EAST SIDE BOYS.

hints.clue: The napkin under the gin was a hiring order, not a round.

title: Day 11 - Hard
headline: THE NAPKIN RING
subheadline: NIGHT EXTRA — After closing time, a sweep of Sterling's booth yielded a crumpled slip from one of his inside men. It proves Sterling knows how the killers breached the study. The note names the weapon, not the man. A hollow silver cane leaned in the study. The face behind it is still a shadow.
originalText: THE KILLER LEANED ON A HOLLOW SILVER CANE.

hints.clue: The booth slip names what leaned in the study, not who held it.

title: Day 12 - Easy
headline: THE HOLLOW CANE
subheadline:
(Newspaper Clipping - The New York Chronicle, Sept 15, 1926)
A major breakthrough in the Vance murder case! Spurred by the precinct's published reward notice, a local pawnshop owner stepped forward this morning with a silver-handled cane matching our description. The owner claims a woman draped in black veils pawned the item for a fraction of its worth. Upon police inspection, the cane was abnormally heavy. I unscrewed the silver ferrule to find a concealed interior. The cipher etched into the silversmith's custom hallmark hints at the cane's true, illicit engineering, confirming it was built to hold a fatal liquid payload.
originalText: THE WALKING STICK WAS A CONCEALED FLASK.

hints.clue: The pawned silver was heavy for a reason.

title: Day 12 - Hard
headline: THE CHEMIST'S BENCH
subheadline: LATE CITY FINAL — The laboratory lamps are still burning. The precinct chemists sent up their preliminary findings in a coded internal wire. We finally know what was inside. The decoded lab report identifies a telltale, distinctively nutty aroma clinging to the interior glass, a classic hallmark of a notorious and lethal poison. If Sterling's crooked chemist mixed those almonds, the fixer already knows. He will keep the carbon.
originalText: TRACES OF BITTER ALMONDS IN THE GLASS TUBE.

hints.clue: The chemists named the smell clinging to the inner glass.

title: Day 13 - Easy
headline: AN EMPTY ROOM
subheadline:
(Journal Entry - Detective Elias Thorne, Sept 16, 1926)
Using the postmarks from Clara's letter, I tracked her hideout to a run-down boarding house in the Bowery. I was too late. The door hung off its hinges, and the small room had been violently tossed. A shattered mirror and a knocked-over chair pointed to a desperate struggle. Clara Vance has been taken. On the remaining shards of the vanity mirror, Clara had scrawled a last line in red lipstick as the door came off its hinges. The letters were smudged, but they did not describe syndicate muscle. The smear points to uniformed hands and steel at her wrists.
originalText: THE WARD WAS DRAGGED OUT IN POLICE HANDCUFFS.

hints.clue: The lipstick on the glass was not syndicate muscle.

title: Day 13 - Hard
headline: THE LIPSTICK GLASS
subheadline: NIGHT EXTRA — Clara’s boarding-house room was empty by moonrise, but she left a longer warning than the lipstick on the glass. If her intel is good, the rot in this town doesn't stop at the docks—it climbs the marble steps. This late dispatch is still in cipher. This sinister cipher confirms that the thugs who took her didn't just act on mob orders—they carried ink-stamped municipal authority to legally drag her away.
originalText: CITY HALL SIGNED THE WARRANT FOR HER ABDUCTION.

hints.clue: The longer warning names municipal ink, not a mob order.

title: Day 14 - Easy
headline: A GRUESOME DISCOVERY
subheadline:
(Police Evidence File - September 17, 1926)
A body was pulled from the East River at dawn. My stomach dropped, fearing it was Clara, but the victim was identified as Reginald, the Vance family butler. He should still have been in my cage. I booked him Saturday night. Chief O'Malley signed him out Sunday morning for insufficient evidence, a handshake and a smirk. Reginald walked thinking he was untouchable. He had fished a planted page from the old man's study books and meant to squeeze Sterling for hush money. His pockets had been violently turned inside out before the water took him, but his stiff fingers still clutched a shredded piece of Cuban silk. Attached to his suspenders was a waterproof oilskin pouch containing that torn ledger page—the same planted books the Coast Guard pulled off The Midnight Runner. He grabbed the wrong sheet. The rifles under the whiskey were not street merchandise. The invoices run to Tammany armories, City Hall's own gun rooms. That page is a warrant to kick down a mayor's door. The killers’ grease-pencil cipher on the back is not his. It is an epitaph for a servant who opened a trap the old man left for someone else, after a purchased Chief cut him loose. The killers' crude handwriting mocks their victim's demands for a payoff, boasting about sending the blackmailing servant to a watery grave.
originalText: THE GREEDY SNITCH SANK TO THE BOTTOM OF THE RIVER.

hints.clue: The river catch still clutched silk and a planted page.

title: Day 14 - Hard
headline: THE STUDY LEDGER
subheadline: LATE CITY FINAL — The missing study manifest reveals Vance wasn't just shipping Havana rum—he was moving crates of military rifles directly into Tammany-controlled wards. When the Feds caught the scent of the armory, the Mayor's office had no choice but to fold.
originalText: THE SMUGGLED RIFLES WENT TO MUNICIPAL ARMORIES.

hints.clue: The missing study book was not about rum.

title: Day 15 - Easy
headline: THE MAYOR STEPS DOWN
subheadline:
(Newspaper Clipping - The Long Island Tattler, Sept 18, 1926)
In a shocking morning press conference, Mayor H. Harrison announced his immediate resignation, citing "sudden and severe health reasons." The city is buzzing with speculation, but our precinct knows the truth. Detective Thorne raided the Mayor’s private office just as the movers were packing his mahogany desk. Hidden in the false bottom of a cigar humidor, Thorne discovered a hidden file Archibald had been keeping on the Mayor’s inner circle. The Mayor’s pristine public image was a house of cards propped up by Tammany Hall fixers, and Vance owned the wind. Thorne has submitted two coded notes found clipped to the Mayor's file to the lab for decryption—messages that reveal the brutal dynamic between the two men. The first decrypted scrap details the sheer extent of Vance's leverage, proving the Mayor was little more than a puppet under the tycoon's total control.
originalText: THE TYCOON HELD THE POLITICIAN BY THE THROAT.

hints.clue: The humidor file shows who owned City Hall.

title: Day 15 - Hard
headline: THE HUMIDOR FILE
subheadline: NIGHT EXTRA — After dark, a second threat arrived from the same blackmail file. This late-city cipher has not been typeset. This night dispatch shifts the crosshairs from municipal hall straight to precinct headquarters, exposing the top lawman's dirty share of the bootlegging pie. That is how the butler walked. O'Malley takes a cut, so the cage never held.
originalText: THE TOP COP TAKES A CUT OF THE SMUGGLING.

hints.clue: The second scrap aims at headquarters, not the mayor's desk.

title: Day 16 - Easy
headline: THE CHIEF'S DILEMMA
subheadline:
(Journal Entry - Detective Elias Thorne, Sept 19, 1926)
With the Mayor stepping down and the Police Chief implicated in the blackmail ring, I realize I cannot trust my own department. I am entirely on my own. That is how Reginald made the river. The Chief cut him loose for Sterling, then routed Clara's execution around my desk. Last night, I broke into the Chief’s private office, searching for any indication of where Clara Vance might have been taken. Under his blotter, I discovered a carbon copy of a secretly intercepted telegraph message, routed away from my desk. It contained orders routing a heavily armed hit squad, and a ticking clock. We must decode it before the hour runs out. The decrypted heading lays bare the tragic scope of the corruption, confirming that every officer on that hit squad is answering to private payrolls.
originalText: THE BADGES ARE BOUGHT AND PAID FOR.

hints.clue: The carbon under the blotter is a payroll, not a warrant.

title: Day 16 - Hard
headline: THE CHIEF'S BLOTTER
subheadline: LATE CITY FINAL — A night courier brought the rest of the blotter orders. The clock is still running. This extra may be her last chance. The second half of the blotter orders targets a specific numbered dock, setting a lethal witching-hour deadline for the hit squad to finish the job.
originalText: THE EXECUTION IS SCHEDULED FOR MIDNIGHT AT PIER FORTY FOUR.

hints.clue: The rest of the blotter names a numbered dock and a witching hour.

title: Day 17 - Easy
headline: SHOOTOUT AT PIER 44
subheadline:
(Newspaper Clipping - The Waterfront Whisperer, Sept 20, 1926)
Gunfire shattered the midnight quiet at Pier 44! A nor'easter had been chewing the Hook since dusk, and the harbor was dark, flooded, and chaotic. A lone, rogue detective survived a fierce ambush on the wet timber. When the powder smoke lifted in the mist, the leader of the hit squad went down hard, and the remaining badges had fled into the night, leaving behind a terrified but unharmed Clara Vance. The missing heiress has finally been found! Thorne escorted her to a secure, undisclosed location. There is no going back to the force now. Rumors say Clara has agreed to testify about the night of her father's murder, and what she witnessed from the secret passage in his study changes the entire investigation. She carried two coded notes she stole from her captors. The stolen note paints a dark picture of the aftermath, commemorating the corrupt officer who met his violent end on the rain-soaked planks.
originalText: A CROOKED STAR LEFT BLEEDING ON THE DOCKS.

hints.clue: The stolen note commemorates a badge that did not leave the planks.

title: Day 17 - Hard
headline: THE WAREHOUSE FLOOR
subheadline: NIGHT EXTRA — The shootout left a second statement on the warehouse floor. Clara stole it from her captors. The second stolen paper exonerates one key suspect from the immediate crime scene, upending our timeline of who actually pulled the trigger.
originalText: ARTHUR NEVER STEPPED FOOT IN THE STUDY.

hints.clue: The warehouse paper clears the surviving partner of the gala room.

title: Day 18 - Easy
headline: THE DAUGHTER'S TALE
subheadline:
(Police Interrogation Transcript - Sept 21, 1926)
Clara sat with a cold cup of black coffee and did not spill a drop. "The priest-hole gives you ears, Detective, but only slivers of sight," she said. "I was not invited. I slipped the panel during the gala. Father never knew I was in the wall. He locked the heavy oak from within—thumb-turn, not the hall key—and sat down to burn the shipping books. He thought the bolt would hold. Then I heard footsteps, the master key draw the bolt back, the door, two people on the rug. Reginald's key threw the same bolt shut from the hallway. A deep voice talked him into a toast before the glass ever left the tray. He drank. He was gone before I could scream. The key turned once more and they walked out." The tremble was gone. What replaced it was a cold, familiar Vance smile. She would not speak the names aloud. She sketched two ciphers instead, mechanical and exact, of how the killers sealed the room she had already survived. Two conspirators, locked in with the man they came to kill, and out again before the cyanide finished its work.
originalText: A PAIR OF WOLVES LOCKED FROM THE INSIDE.

hints.clue: Two came in after the bolt, and two went out before the glass finished.

title: Day 18 - Hard
headline: THE PRIEST-HOLE
subheadline: LATE CITY FINAL — After dusk Clara dictated a longer cipher: the rest of what she could swear to. The talk came first—a clinical cadence, a toast offered like a dose. The glass followed. Cyanide does not wait. By the time the coupe sat centered on the desk, the old man was already gone.
originalText: THE SHADOW SPOKE WITH A CLINICAL TONE.

hints.clue: The toast was offered like a dose, not a celebration.

title: Day 19 - Easy
headline: THE DOCTOR RETURNS
subheadline:
(Journal Entry - Detective Elias Thorne, Sept 22, 1926)
A deep voice. A carved silver cane. A shadow Clara could not name. I brought in an abandoned leather kit recovered from a Grand Central locker and popped the latches. The sharp stench of sanatorium narcotics hit the room instantly, alongside a frantic, handwritten note: "I secured the cyanide, Bea. We take his money tonight." A travel stub under the lining used a name that was not his. Clara’s hands began to shake violently—the sensory shock tore straight through her drug haze. "That smell... that voice in the study." The horrifying math clicked. He took a phantom train down, played the phantom at the gala, and went back to his Albany desk. I had been looking for a mobster. I had already shaken the killer's hand. This is the first paper that puts the Albany physician in the mansion on gala night.
originalText: A TRAVEL ALIAS PROVES HE WAS AT THE GALA.

hints.clue: The stub in the kit used a name that was not the physician's.

title: Day 19 - Hard
headline: THE MEDICAL BAG
subheadline: NIGHT EXTRA — A night search of the medical bag produced a second cipher revealing exactly what the doctor brought to the gala. This second cipher specifies the exact fatal compound the physician smuggled into the mansion to fuel his lover's deadly scheme.
originalText: HE SUPPLIED THE CYANIDE FOR HER PLOT.

hints.clue: The second paper in the bag names what he carried to the mansion.

title: Day 20 - Easy
headline: LOVERS ON THE RUN
subheadline:
(Newspaper Clipping - The New York Chronicle, Sept 23, 1926)
A city-wide manhunt is underway for socialite Beatrice Vance and Dr. Aris Blackwood. Most of the city was glued to the radio broadcast of the Dempsey-Tunney heavyweight bout last night, leaving the streets practically deserted. Detective Thorne used the distraction to breach Beatrice's Plaza Hotel suite, only to find the wall safe emptied. A terrified maid reported seeing the pair fleeing toward the harbor, noting the doctor looked pale and frantic while Beatrice stared at him with cold, predatory eyes. The murderous lovers have made their escape, but a discarded telegraph draft in their wastebasket reveals their desperate destination. The recovered telegraph draft outlines the pair's escape vector, revealing their flight route toward warmer, unpoliced waters.
originalText: THE GUILTY BIRDS ARE FLYING SOUTH.

hints.clue: The wastebasket draft names a warmer heading, not a courtroom.

title: Day 20 - Hard
headline: THE LEATHER TRUNK
subheadline: LATE CITY FINAL — Harbor pilots report a steamer clearing with a leather trunk in the hold. Decode the night extra before it clears the Hook. The trunk is a dummy. The pair never boarded. A black Packard left the Plaza after the fight, and the doctor was already arguing in the passenger seat—cold feet, a split he wanted, a southbound run without her.
originalText: THE MURDERERS ARE NOT ON THAT BOAT.

hints.clue: The trunk in the hold is a dummy; watch the Packard, not the steamer.

title: Day 21 - Easy
headline: THE BAIT IS SET
subheadline:
(Journal Entry - Detective Elias Thorne, Sept 24, 1926)
With the local police force hopelessly compromised—and my own Chief dead by my hand at Pier 44—Clara and I cannot simply walk into a precinct. We need the rats to eat each other. I did not invent the gold. I found a telegraph the old man left in the open, a shipping line pointing at Pier 84 and a fortune that was supposed to move after dark. I took it for bait. I leaked two rumors through a trusted dockworker. One of them concerns a massive, unguarded offshore gold payout moving through Pier 84. Phantom fortune. No guards. They will both come armed, each expecting to collect the vault that is not theirs. We chose Pier 84 for the trap. A midnight rendezvous has been staged by a single lantern. I only hope their greed outweighs their caution. Harbor men still have the Packard circling the west-side slips. The doctor is in it. Beatrice has not let him out since the Plaza. She will not split that gold. I dispatched my dockyard contacts to spread the bait. They just routed back an encoded slip from the waterfront. The bait is no longer a rumor in our mouths. Someone with a fleet and a payroll is already moving men toward the lantern. I think I am striking a match. I do not yet know who laid the kindling.
originalText: THE RUMOR PROMISED OFFSHORE GOLD AT THE DOCKS.

hints.clue: The dockworker leak was bait about a fortune that would never sail.

title: Day 21 - Hard
headline: THE SECOND RUMOR
subheadline: NIGHT EXTRA — A second courier slip went out after the morning rumor. Decode this night dispatch before the lantern is lit. Heavy guns in the fog means someone is already moving. The old man left them a city that runs on greed; they are still playing checkers for gold he moved off the board years ago.
originalText: HEAVY ARTILLERY IS COMING IN THE FOG.

hints.clue: The second slip is not about gold. It is about guns in the mist.

title: Day 22 - Easy
headline: A SHOCKING ARRIVAL
subheadline:
(Police Evidence File - Narrative Account, Sept 25, 1926)
The trap at Pier 84 was set. Clara stood by a single flickering lantern, clutching a decoy ledger. I was perched high above in the rusted iron rafters, my revolver drawn. A sleek black Packard silently rolled onto the damp wooden docks. The driver's door swung wide, but it wasn't Sterling who stepped into the lamplight. It was the widow, wrapped in mink, her silhouette cutting through the mist. In the passenger seat sat a shadowy figure who never moved. She had kept him there since the Plaza, pale and arguing, until he was no longer useful. Beatrice laughed coldly into the fog as her hand emerged from her coat. She didn't come to negotiate. I had seen enough: the widow brought gunpowder, not lawyers.
originalText: THE WIDOW BROUGHT LEAD INSTEAD OF LAWYERS.

hints.clue: The mink on the planks did not come to negotiate.

title: Day 22 - Hard
headline: THE PACKARD DOOR
subheadline: LATE CITY FINAL — When the smoke cleared over the Packard, detectives found Dr. Blackwood slumped in the front seat, his own gun drawn but unfired. He had been clinging to her since the Plaza, begging for a split and a southbound berth. She let him ride shotgun until the phantom gold was in sight, then spent him. The powder burns on the doctor's lapel are close-range. This was not a panic shot. She decided it the night they left the hotel. She killed him for loot the dead man had already taken off the board.
originalText: SHE SLAUGHTERED THE DOCTOR TO KEEP ALL THE LOOT.

hints.clue: The powder on the passenger’s lapel was close-range, and not panic.

title: Day 23 - Easy
headline: HONOR AMONG THIEVES
subheadline:
(Journal Entry - Detective Elias Thorne, Sept 26, 1926)
Before Beatrice could pull the trigger, I dropped a flash flare from the rafters, allowing Clara to scramble behind heavy iron freight crates as the shadows around the Packard shifted. Arthur Sterling stepped forward with his hired guns, exactly as I had baited him. He knew someone was setting a trap, and as the two rival crews collided in the fog, Sterling smugly shifted his position, revealing a brutal tactical advantage to ensure his own survival. Mob enforcers and Beatrice’s remaining muscle melted out of the fog, surrounding the desperate pair, guns drawn. I stayed in the rafters and let the wolves work. A standoff held on the rotting planks of the pier. From the iron I watched Sterling's cowardice in full: he dragged Beatrice into the line of fire and used her as a human shield.
originalText: USING THE MOTHER AS A HUMAN SHIELD.

hints.clue: From the rafters, the surviving partner found a coward’s cover.

title: Day 23 - Hard
headline: FROM THE RAFTERS
subheadline: NIGHT EXTRA — Honor among thieves lasted until moonrise. This cipher is what Thorne overheard from the rafters. Sterling is not waving a bottle. He is waving a shop ticket. He bought the chemist to keep Clara quiet on morphine. Blackwood, cheap and arrogant, used that same crooked bench for bitter almonds and a hollow cane. After the lab named the almonds, Sterling kept the carbon to hang the doctor if the cops ever got too close. He was never in the study. He just kept the paper.
originalText: ARTHUR KEPT THE APOTHECARY RECEIPT FOR BLACKMAIL.

hints.clue: He is waving a shop ticket, not a bottle.

title: Day 24 - Easy
headline: AFTER THE BLOOD
subheadline:
(Newspaper Clipping - The New York Chronicle, Sept 27, 1926)
By the time the sirens reached Pier 84, the rival factions had already shredded one another in the harbor's gloom. Detective Thorne did not call his old precinct. He arranged the meeting so Sterling’s mob and Beatrice’s hired guns would do the killing for him, sitting in the rafters until the shooting slowed. Only then did his timed tip bring a different breed of authorities swarming over the docks to handle the gruesome aftermath. Beatrice Vance dropped what was left of her Derringer and wept for a lawyer. Arthur Sterling attempted to sprint toward a waiting speedboat, but Thorne finally came down from the iron and tackled him to the dock, sending his loaded revolver plunging into the dark waters of the Hudson River. The reign of the Vance & Sterling crime syndicate has violently ended. Thorne's calculated delay ensured federal agents arrived just in time to clear the dock floor and take over the crime scene. He would later write that he had not closed a murder. He had executed a dead man's vengeance.
originalText: LET THE FEDS SWEEP UP THE BODIES.

hints.clue: The sirens were timed. He let another badge mop the dock.

title: Day 24 - Hard
headline: THE TREASURY CLEANUP
subheadline: LATE CITY FINAL — The harbor cleanup is not the last chapter. A final piece of paper fluttered from Sterling's coat during the struggle. This late cipher hints at a massive unresolved loose end. Treasury is mopping a board the old man set three years ago. The dropped paper exposes a critical financial loose end, confirming that the syndicate's vast wealth remains hidden far from public view.
originalText: THE SYNDICATE ACCOUNTS ARE STILL BURIED.

hints.clue: The paper from the coat is a ledger, not a surrender.

title: Day 25 - Easy
headline: A CONFESSION UNDER NEON
subheadline:
(Police Interrogation Transcript - Federal Bureau, Sept 28, 1926)
Sitting under the buzzing neon of the federal holding tank, Arthur Sterling finally cracked. With his dock muscle behind bars, the arrogance was gone. "I'm a bootlegger, not a butcher," he spat, pointing at the two-way glass. "The doctor walked the cane over the threshold. The widow poured the glass. I was on the ballroom floor in plain view of fifty guests!" Clara watched through the two-way glass without flinching as Sterling slid a feverish, encoded confession across the table, revealing exactly how the poison was administered. The bootlegger's signed statement pins the act directly on Beatrice, attesting that she personally laced and served her husband's final glass.
originalText: THE WIFE SERVED THE DEADLY VINTAGE.

hints.clue: Under neon he names who poured the last glass.

title: Day 25 - Hard
headline: THE SECOND SIGNATURE
subheadline: NIGHT EXTRA — After the lights dimmed in the interrogation room he added a second cipher. Clara watched from behind the two-way glass and did not flinch. The confession names the pieces. Archibald arranged the board so they would take each other. This secondary admission legally seals the widow's mastermind role, cornering her into one final, desperate play.
originalText: A SIGNED CONFESSION PINS THE MASTERMIND.

hints.clue: The second signature is meant to corner her, not him.

title: Day 26 - Easy
headline: THE WIDOW'S LAST STAND
subheadline:
(Newspaper Clipping - The Waterfront Whisperer, Sept 29, 1926)
In federal custody, Beatrice Vance attempted one final, desperate play. She demanded a private meeting with the government's lead attorney, leaning in close to whisper a scandalous proposition, casually checking her reflection in the interrogation mirror while bargaining with a man's life. The prosecutor was unswayed. Detective Thorne bribed the court stenographer for a carbon copy of the transcript, which I ran through a Treasury cipher desk to keep it off municipal blotters. The trial of the century begins tomorrow, and the city's corrupt elite are trembling as subpoenas are handed out like candy. The intercepted transcript details Beatrice's attempt to buy her freedom, offering her illicit fortune in exchange for dropped charges.
originalText: OFFERING BLOOD MONEY FOR CLEMENCY.

hints.clue: She tried to buy the prosecutor with a fortune she did not own.

title: Day 26 - Hard
headline: THE VAULT INVENTORY
subheadline: LATE CITY FINAL — A night inventory of the secured assets produced a shocking ledger. This final line is the one the morning paper would not print. The vault was never Beatrice's to offer. Archibald parked the overseas fortune in the daughter's name years ago, left a map in the open, and let the syndicate run a company they did not own. Thorne thought he invented bait. He only struck the match the old man laid. He was playing chess while they were playing checkers. The confidential audit drops a major bombshell, revealing that the syndicate's overseas fortune was secretly locked away in the name of the tycoon's own flesh and blood.
originalText: THE OFFSHORE VAULT BELONGS TO THE DAUGHTER.

hints.clue: The night inventory finds the fortune parked in another name.

title: Day 27 - Easy
headline: THE TRIAL OF THE CENTURY
subheadline:
(Journal Entry - Detective Elias Thorne, Sept 30, 1926)
The supreme court gallery was packed to the rafters as the joint capital murder trial of Arthur Sterling and Beatrice Vance commenced. Photographers' flashbulbs popped like firecrackers as Clara Vance took the witness stand. Dressed in a modest navy suit, she recounted her father’s murder and her harrowing abduction with a poise that captured the courtroom's sympathy instantly. Sterling’s high-priced attorneys attempted to poke holes in my rogue investigation, but the federal prosecutor introduced Exhibit A—Thorne's most damning piece of physical evidence recovered from the waterfront. The jury has the case. I am waiting in the gallery for the slip of paper that ends it. The prosecutor's critical evidence submission delivers the decisive blow, using recovered financial records to seal both defendants' fates.
originalText: THE BOOTLEGGING LEDGER SEALS THEIR FATE.

hints.clue: Exhibit A is a waterfront book, not a witness's nerves.

title: Day 27 - Hard
headline: THE PROSECUTOR'S SLIP
subheadline: NIGHT EXTRA — The jury was out less than an hour. A second encoded note from the prosecutor’s table records what the morning extras could not wait for. The chair is the last square on a board he set when he signed the dead-man's trust. He did not arrange the gala glass. He arranged what the glass would cost them.
originalText: A GUILTY VERDICT DEMANDS THE ELECTRIC CHAIR.

hints.clue: The jury was out less than an hour; the slip names the sentence.

title: Day 28 - Easy
headline: THE SECRET INHERITANCE
subheadline:
(Police Evidence File - Narrative Account, Oct 1, 1926)
With the jury deliberating Beatrice’s fate, Clara returned to the quiet estate escorted by Detective Thorne. Waiting in the study was Archibald's private attorney, holding a brass lockbox stamped with instructions to open only upon Vance's unnatural death. This was not a 1923 handover of keys. It was a dead-man's trust. The patents, the fleet, and the board stayed in the wolves' hands for three years so they would keep siphoning a company they never owned. Beatrice spent months conspiring to murder her husband for control of the shipping line, but Archibald had anticipated the wolves at his throat long before the night of the gala. Inside the box rested a single coded directive in the tycoon's handwriting. Archibald's posthumous directive reveals that the rights to his inventions and his entire maritime fleet were legally transferred out of his wife's reach long before she ever plotted her move.
originalText: THE PATENTS AND SHIPS WERE SIGNED OVER YEARS AGO.

hints.clue: The brass box was a dead-man's trust, not a handover of keys.

title: Day 28 - Hard
headline: THE DEAD MAN'S HAND
subheadline: LATE CITY FINAL — Among Archibald’s papers Thorne found a longer cipher in the dead man’s hand. This is his last night letter. He had been laying the trap for years, not staging the night they came. He thought a deadbolt and a grate full of shipping books would buy him until morning. He was wrong about the door. He was not wrong about the board. The wolves killed a man who had already spent them.
originalText: THE OLD MAN ENGINEERED HIS OWN REVENGE.

hints.clue: His last night letter is about the board, not the bolt that failed.

title: Day 29 - Easy
headline: A NEW DAWN
subheadline:
(Newspaper Clipping - The New York Chronicle, Oct 2, 1926)
A crisp autumn wind blew off the harbor as Clara Vance stood before the headquarters of the newly renamed Vance Maritime Company. Her first act as sole proprietor took place behind closed doors with the company ledgers. She worked through the night with a red pen, issuing a series of unyielding directives to sever the company's darkest ties. Detective Thorne watched from the docks as the reformed fleet departed the harbor. The rot looked cut out of New York. Thorne’s smile did not quite reach his eyes. There were still a few lines left in his journal. Her midnight reforms focus directly on the shipping paperwork, systematically erasing every criminal connection from the company manifests.
originalText: PURGING THE SYNDICATE FROM THE MANIFESTS.

hints.clue: Her first act as proprietor was a red pen on the shipping books.

title: Day 29 - Hard
headline: AFTER THE DOCKS WENT QUIET
subheadline: NIGHT EXTRA — After the docks went quiet, Thorne watched Clara at her father’s old grate. Decode what he wrote down. She is not locking the last of the old man's files away. She is feeding them to the fire. Those were papers he planted. He did not lose the files. He spent them.
originalText: CLARA BURNED THE FINAL BLACKMAIL LEDGER IN THE FURNACE.

hints.clue: At the old grate she is not filing the last papers. She is feeding them.

title: Day 30 - Easy
headline: CASE CLOSED
subheadline:
(Journal Entry - Detective Elias Thorne, Oct 3, 1926)
I sit in my favorite diner, watching the rain wash the city streets clean. I left my tarnished badge on the counter to pay for the coffee. The Vance case is officially closed. Arthur Sterling and Beatrice Vance sit in Sing Sing’s death cells awaiting the electric chair, and Mayor Harrison’s corrupt administration is nothing but a disgraced memory. After Pier 44, there is no precinct that would have me, and none I would have back. Before she left for a tour of Europe, Clara Vance sent me a small, heavy package containing a parting gift, and an envelope containing two final ciphers. The first cipher named the price of the gift. It was not a thank-you for keeping her safe. It’s a quiet morning. New York feels safer. I know better than to call it honest. The heavy package reveals a ticking, gilded token of gratitude, a beautiful but grim reminder of the violent toll and spent shell casings it took to earn it.
originalText: A GOLD WATCH BOUGHT WITH BLOOD AND BRASS.

hints.clue: The heavy package ticks, and it is not a thank-you note.

title: Day 30 - Hard
headline: CLARA'S LAST ENVELOPE
subheadline: LATE CITY FINAL — The diner was quiet this morning. Clara’s last envelope, opened under the night lamps of the Chronicle composing room, contains no thank-you. It is a sailing notice: a berth booked under ink that is not her own, and a ship already clearing the Hook. The old man bought her that exit when he signed the trust. The last square was always hers.
originalText: CLARA BOARDED A STEAMSHIP FOR PARIS UNDER A FALSE NAME.

hints.clue: The last envelope is a sailing notice, booked in ink that is not hers.
